To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
humans are very sensitive to discriminate short square reductions of the frictional force during active tactile exploration.

the human perception is very sensitive to the duration and transition time of square ultrasonic reductions in friction and that the perception of the same ultrasonic signal can be different depending on the speed of finger motion.
humans can perceive square ultrasonic reductions and that the perception of these reductions depends on their sharpness, duration and the speed of finger motion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the human perception of transient changes in frictional cues.
the human perception of transient changes of surface friction.
the perception of transient frictional cues in the context of active tactile exploration and with the role of frictional dynamics on the perception of transient changes in friction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the perception of square reductions is a combination of the perception of the edges and the perception of the frictional reduction.
square reductions of friction with sharp transitions are perceived as edges and can therefore be used to convey information to the user about object features.
the human perception is not only dependent on the friction reduction but also on its shape, duration, and speed of exploration, which are all factors that should be considered in future applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the human perception is very sensitive to transient frictional changes, and the perception of square reductions in friction can be influenced by their sharpness, duration as well as by the speed of exploration, which is in line with the previous findings.
ultrasonic square reductions of friction with variable transition time and duration can induce different perception of frictional cues during active tactile exploration.
ultrasonic modulation of friction is perceived by humans as a reduction in friction, which is dependent on the sharpness and duration of the frictional cue and on the speed of the finger exploration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human sensitivity to ultrasonic modulations of friction can be used for the design of new vibrotactile displays.
the human perception is very sensitive to the sharpness and duration of square reductions of finger surface friction.
the human tactile system is sensitive to the sharpness and duration of square reductions of the friction and can use this information to discriminate different transient frictional cues.
